svg.text: Little Aeronauts: How Spiders Fly on Electricity
a gossamer plate — tiptoe, fan, field, and a ship sixty miles from shore · seed 20261021
A · The Tiptoe Test
testing the air
one leg raised —
a weather station
anchor dragline,
kept until lift wins
A · First, climb highest. Then stand on tiptoe,
abdomen to the sky, and interrogate the air.
B · The Fan, Not a Parachute
strands repel — like charges spread the fan
up to ~60 fibres · most ~200 nm across · metres long
B · No single sail: dozens of nanoscale fibres,
where the air itself turns sticky, like honey.
C · The Invisible Weather
earth: negative
sky: positive
sharp tips
concentrate it
fair weather ≈ 120 V per metre
storms: kilovolts / m
C · A permanent voltage lives between ground
and sky — spiders read it like we read wind.
D · The Bristol Switch (2018)
sealed box · no airflow
field ON ↑ · OFF ↓
trichobothria —
hairs that feel
electric fields
Erigone money spiders tiptoed when the field
was switched on — and settled when it stopped.
D · Turn the invisible weather on, and a wingless
animal prepares to fly. Turn it off, it lands.
E · Sixty Miles from Shore
HMS Beagle · 31 Oct – 1 Nov 1832
“some thousands on the ship” — Darwin
each ~one-tenth of an inch, dusky red
E · They arrived under their own silk, at sea,
with a rapidity Darwin called unaccountable.
F · First Ashore
Krakatau, May 1884 — nine months after the
eruption, the only living thing found: a spider
F · On sterilised islands, life's first scout
so often arrives by air, on a thread.
Plate XVII · Little Aeronauts — Lapis, atelier, October 21, 2026
